note: Editorial and decision layer for the marketing set. Facts quoted here were read off the official pages listed in `verified_utc` of each item; anything not stated on an official page is labelled as an editorial judgement or left out. This file drives marketing/index.html, the topic articles, and the improvements board. It is generated markup only - no page is hand-edited.

brand.name: Counter Notes
brand.sub: Countertop cooking gear, read off the spec sheet
brand.standfirst: We read the manufacturer page and the Amazon listing, put the numbers side by side, and tell you which one to buy. No unboxing, no invented opinions - and we say which numbers the brands never published.
brand.footer_note: Counter Notes is an independent editorial project. We may earn a commission when you buy through links on this site - at no extra cost to you. That never changes what a product's specification says, and it is why every row on this site links to the page it came from.

voice.brief: Write like a specialist who has read every page of the manual and is telling a friend what to buy: short sentences, real numbers, an opinion, and no adjectives doing work a number could do.

rules.rule: Open with the decision, not with the category
rules.do: How many quarts you need depends on how many people you cook for - and on whether you reheat or roast. Here is the arithmetic on all three spec sheets.
rules.dont: In today's fast-paced kitchen, air fryers have become an essential appliance for modern home cooks.
rules.why: Generic scene-setting is the single strongest AI tell, and it is also the paragraph a reader skips. Google's own guidance is to publish non-commodity content and not to recycle what a generative model could produce.

rules.rule: Every factual sentence carries its source
rules.do: The 6 Qt model runs to 450 degrees F in Hi-Fry (Chefman spec page).
rules.dont: It gets hotter than most rivals for maximum crispiness.
rules.why: A claim with no source is either a guess or marketing copy. On this site a sentence with a number is a row in a table, and the table row ends in the page it came from.

rules.rule: Separate the measurement from the judgement, visibly
rules.do: Put the opinion in a labelled box, and say what it rests on.
rules.dont: Naturally, this is the best choice for families.
rules.why: Readers can forgive a wrong opinion. They cannot forgive an opinion presented as a spec. The gate checks the label is present, so an unlabelled judgement fails the build.

rules.do: It is the widest of the three: 15.8 in across.
rules.dont: This groundbreaking, game-changing appliance revolutionises your cooking.
rules.why: Superlatives are unfalsifiable and are the second strongest AI tell. A measurement is falsifiable, so it is worth more to a reader and to search.

rules.rule: Name the number the brand did not publish
rules.do: Neither official page states an inner-basket material or a clearance requirement, so those rows are blank - not guessed.
rules.dont: Silence, or a plausible filler value.
rules.why: Admitting a gap is the cheapest trust signal available and the one almost no affiliate site uses. It is also the site's standing rule: blank beats inferred.

rules.rule: One sentence, one idea; average under 20 words
rules.do: Both baskets finish together. Chefman calls it Sync Finish.
rules.dont: Featuring an innovative dual-basket design, this appliance ensures that both baskets are cooked to perfection simultaneously, thereby eliminating the need to manage multiple timers.
rules.why: Stacked subordinate clauses and -ing participles are the mechanical rhythm of generated text. Short declarative sentences read as a person thinking.

rules.do: A 13.3 lb box on a 10.6 in tall frame.
rules.dont: A substantial build with considered dimensions.
rules.why: Numbers and nouns are checkable; abstractions are not, and abstractions are where generated filler hides.

rules.rule: Say who it is NOT for
rules.do: Skip this one if your counter is under 16 in deep - it is the widest of the three.
rules.dont: A perfect fit for anyone and everyone.
rules.why: A recommendation that excludes nobody helps nobody and converts nobody. The point of the site is the click that follows a decision, and a decision needs a reason to say no.

rules.rule: No invented testing, no invented author
rules.do: State what we did: read the official pages on a date, quote them, and mark what they disagree about.
rules.dont: Our team tested this for three weeks.
rules.why: Nobody has used these products (Q-11 on the programme board is unanswered). A fake hands-on claim is both a false statement to readers and outside the limits the Associates Programme Policies set for representing Amazon content.

rules.rule: Never print a price or a star rating
rules.do: Link through to the listing, where Amazon serves its own current price.
rules.dont: It is rated 4.4 stars by thousands of happy customers - an excellent choice for anyone.
rules.why: Amazon's rules restrict displaying prices except through the mechanisms Amazon serves, and ratings are volatile and storefront-specific. The deploy gate fails the build on a money figure in a buying context.

design.summary: A magazine front page with a data spine: wide measure of prose, spec tables that never leave the reading column, one accent colour used only for links and status, and no cards for content that is not a card.
tokens: Serif headline stack for article titles, system sans for UI, tabular numerals in tables. Body measure 66ch, line-height 1.55.
Paper #fff / ink #14181f / rule #e3e6ea / accent #b4472a (used for links, the take box and status only). No gradient, no shadow except a 1px hairline on hover.
Single column at the reading width; the sidebar carries navigation only. Breakpoints 1080 / 820 / 520. Nothing important is below the fold on mobile.
Spec table, take box, blank-row (dash + reason), citation sup, status pill, article card with a number in it (not a stock photo).
None beyond a hover state. No carousel, no autoplay, no cookie wall, no popup.
Product photography is not licensed to us. Until the image question on the programme board is answered, the visual identity is typographic: big numbers, rules and whitespace.
Landmarks, skip link, visible focus ring, contrast ratio above 4.5:1 for body text, tables with real th/scope and captions.

One CSS file, no webfont download, no third-party JS, no analytics on the marketing set until a consent posture is decided. Reader-facing pages must stay under 60 kB of HTML each; the improvement board is exempt because it is an owner surface, and its size is stated on the page.
anti_patterns: A hero band with three equal cards, each with an icon in a circle - the default look of every generated site.
Stock photography of a person smiling at a laptop.
A row of four identical KPI counters on a consumer page.
Section headings that are the words Overview, Features, Introduction.
A disclosure written as a legal paragraph in 11 px grey: it must read as a person talking to the reader, and still say the mandatory sentence.

guides.title: How many quarts of air fryer do you actually need?
guides.meta_description: 6 Qt, 8 Qt and 26 Qt, measured against what each manufacturer says the basket is sized for. The arithmetic, not a rule of thumb - plus the numbers neither brand publishes.
guides.target_query: what size air fryer do i need
guides.hook: Capacity is the one number every buyer looks at and almost nobody can translate. Six quarts of what? Here is the only honest way to answer it: read what each manufacturer says its own basket is sized for, and then do the arithmetic on the dimensions, because the quarts figure is measured by the brand and no two measure it the same way.
guides.angle: Every competitor answers this with a rule of thumb for everybody. We answer it for these three specific models, with the published servings claim beside the internal dimensions, and we mark the rows where the brand never published a servings figure at all.

sections.h2: What the three pages actually claim

blocks.html: Two of the three manufacturers put a household size next to the capacity. The third puts nothing: its page states a quart figure and stops. That absence is the most useful thing on the page, because it tells you who is expected to cook in it.

The 6 Qt dual-basket model is the only one of the three that never publishes a servings number on its product page. Chefman publishes instead two independent 3 Qt baskets and a Sync Finish function that ends both baskets at the same moment - which is a different answer to the same question: this is a machine for cooking two things at once, not a machine for cooking a lot of one thing.

sections.h2: Use the box, not the badge

blocks.html: Quarts are measured by the brand. Dimensions are not negotiable: 13.38 x 11.81 x 10.63 in is the space the 6 Qt unit needs, and 15.8 in across is the width of the Emeril. If the cabinet above your counter is 14 in of clearance, the tall fryer oven is out no matter what its capacity claim says.

Measure your counter depth and the height of the lowest obstruction above it before you compare any two capacity figures. Then compare capacity. On all three of these pages, the footprint number is the one that will make the decision for you.

One thing none of the three publishes: a minimum clearance requirement for ventilation. That row is blank on our tables and it is not a secret - the information is simply not on the official product pages. If the clearance number matters in your kitchen, it comes from the instruction manual, which is a document we have not been given and will not quote from memory.

sections.h2: Rule of thumb, for what it is worth

items: One or two people, mostly reheating: the smallest of these is enough, and a second basket buys you nothing.
Four to six people: both the 8 Qt basket and the 26 Qt oven publish that household size, and they reach it by opposite routes - one big batch, or an oven that roasts.
Two dishes that finish together: only the dual-basket model publishes that function, and it is the reason that design exists.

blocks.html: The first and third lines are an editorial judgement about the two verified rows beside them, not a manufacturer instruction. The middle line is a quotation: the Emeril page says its 26-quart capacity is for preparing food for four to six people, and the Chefman 8 Qt page says it is designed for four to six people.

guides.title: Two baskets or one big one? A trade you cannot undo later
guides.meta_description: A 6 Qt twin-basket fryer against an 8 Qt single: what you gain in timing, what you lose in volume, and the two specs that decide it.
guides.target_query: dual basket air fryer vs single basket
guides.hook: The dual-basket pitch is not really about capacity. It is about finishing two foods at the same time, which is a timing problem, not a volume problem. Once you see it that way, the comparison gets much easier - and one of these two stops being the sensible default for most kitchens.
guides.angle: Nobody else frames it as a timing trade rather than a size trade, and the two models here are close enough in watts (both 1700 W) that the design is the only real difference between them.

sections.h2: The two machines, in the numbers they publish

blocks.html: Same power budget - 1700 W on both - and different top temperature: the dual-window model goes to 450 F using its Hi-Fry setting, the single-basket model's published range stops at 400 F. In a twin-basket design, 1700 W is split across two chambers; in a single chamber, all of it works on one volume of air. Neither page states a per-basket wattage, so that is the shape of the trade-off, not a measurement.

sections.h2: What Sync Finish buys you

blocks.html: Chefman describes the function directly: both baskets finish cooking at the same time, and the two 3 Qt baskets are independent. Two independent baskets with a synchronised end is the whole argument for the design. It is a two-dish machine, and it is a 3 Qt machine twice, not a 6 Qt machine.

Buy the twin basket if your real problem is that the chicken is ready before the fries are. Buy the single 8 Qt if your problem is that one batch is not enough for the table. If both problems are yours, you are shopping for a bigger kitchen, not a different fryer.

sections.h2: Where the single basket wins on paper

blocks.html: The 8 Qt has the larger chamber (7.57 L against two 3 Qt halves), a whole-food volume no split basket reaches, and a four-preset panel - fries, chicken, fish, meat - that the manufacturer lists in that order. It also has an LED shake reminder, which the dual-window page does not mention, and a documented auto shut-off that stops cooking when the timer runs out or the basket is pulled.
The dual-window page answers with two features the 8 Qt page does not claim: viewing windows on both baskets with an interior light, and a 450 F maximum.

guides.title: Air fryer or air fryer toaster oven: the door is the decision
guides.meta_description: A basket fryer and a 26 Qt French-door fryer oven, compared on the specs that matter: door, rack space, modes and temperature range.
guides.target_query: air fryer vs air fryer toaster oven
guides.hook: Basket, or oven with doors? Most comparisons answer with a list of extra modes. That is the wrong first question. The mechanical difference is the door: a basket you pull out, or a front that swings open so a sheet pan can slide in. Everything else follows from that, including which of them can roast a chicken.
guides.angle: The Emeril page is unusually explicit about its door and its 26-quart interior, which lets us tie the mode list to the geometry instead of reciting it.

sections.h2: The door, because it decides everything else

blocks.html: The Emeril page describes dual French doors that open for access to a 26 Qt chamber, sized on the manufacturer's own tile for preparing food for four to six people, with a dual-speed fan for crisping and 360-degree hot-air circulation. A basket fryer cannot offer that geometry: the food sits in a drawer, and the drawer sets the maximum size of what fits.
The basket model's counter-argument is also on its page, and it is a good one: two independent baskets, a viewing window on each, an interior light, and a 450 F top temperature.

sections.h2: Ten modes, and what the list is really for

blocks.html: The Emeril lists ten functions on its page: Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Defrost, Dehydrate, Grill, Proof, Reheat, Roast, Warm. Read as a sentence it is marketing; read as a set of racks and elements it is a specification. Bake, Broil and Roast need chamber height. Dehydrate and Proof need a low end of the temperature scale. The basket fryers here publish a range starting at 200 F; the oven publishes one starting at 75 F.

blocks.caption: Published temperature range and control type, with the official page for each.
head: Model
Range (as published)

blocks.html: If you want one appliance to replace a second oven, the low end and the height of the chamber matter more than how many verbs the box prints. If you want crispy frozen food fast, a basket reaches temperature with less empty air to heat and a third of the counter.

guides.title: Hi-Fry, 450 F and 400 F: why two official pages disagree about one fryer
guides.meta_description: The Amazon title for Chefman's 8 Qt fryer advertises a 450 F Hi-Fry option; the manufacturer's 8 Qt page states 200-400 F. Both pages, one table, and what we publish.
guides.target_query: what is hi-fry on a Chefman air fryer
guides.hook: On one product, Amazon's title says the Hi-Fry option reaches 450 F. The manufacturer's own page for the same model states a range that stops at 400 F. This is not a typo you can pick a side of. It is a difference between a listing written for a category and a specification written for a machine - and it is exactly the kind of thing a buying decision should be made around, not through.
guides.angle: The two statements are both verbatim from official pages, we quote both, and we publish the number the manufacturer states while flagging the listing. Very few affiliate posts will show you their disagreement.

sections.h2: What Hi-Fry is, on the page that defines it

blocks.html: On the 6 Qt dual-window page, Chefman lists a maximum temperature of 450 F / 235 C with the Hi-Fry function. So the function is a temperature ceiling - an above-normal setting for a finishing stage, not a separate cooking mode. The same brand's 8 Qt page states its range as 200-400 F, with no Hi-Fry figure printed in the specification block.

sections.h2: Where the 450 F on the listing comes from

blocks.html: We do not know, and we are not going to guess. What is verifiable: the Amazon title for the 8 Qt reads TurboFry 4-in-1 with 450 F Hi-Fry Option for Crispier Results, while the manufacturer's specification for that model states 200-400 F. One of the two is describing a different variant, and neither page says which.

blocks.caption: The same attribute, as published by two official sources.
head: Which page
What it states about the maximum temperature
rows: 450 F Hi-Fry option for crispier results
Max temp: 450 F / 235 C with Hi-Fry function

blocks.html: For the 8 Qt we publish 400 F, because a specification block outranks a search title, and a listing written by a reseller is not a manufacturer spec. For the 6 Qt we publish 450 F, because that is what the manufacturer's own feature list states for that model. If you need a Hi-Fry setting on the counter, buy the model whose own page prints it.

sections.h2: What this means for a shopping list

blocks.html: Treat a temperature in a product title as a claim to be checked against the specification, on this brand and on every brand. Where the two disagree, we mark the row CONFLICT in the tables on this site rather than quietly choosing one number - the same row you are reading is the one that took us a day to settle.

guides.title: Will it fit? The exact footprint of all three, in inches
guides.meta_description: 13.38 x 11.81 x 10.63 in and 13.3 lb against 15.4 x 12.6 x 13.5 in and 12.8 lb, against a 26 Qt oven at 16.9 in deep. The dimensions table, with the weight and the blanks.
guides.hook: Return reasons are usually not performance. They are the cupboard, the splash-back and the height of the cabinet above the counter. So before the capacity debate: here are the three sets of numbers that decide whether the machine is going to live on your counter or in a car park queue at the returns desk.
guides.angle: Every figure below is transcribed from the product page, in both units where the page gives both, with the weight that has to be lifted onto a shelf. The blanks are labelled, and one of them is the number shoppers ask for most.

sections.h2: Dimensions and weight, as published
The three questions the pages do not answer

items: How much clearance the manufacturer wants around the vents - not stated on any of the three product pages.
Whether the door swing needs front clearance on the 26 Qt oven - the page describes dual French doors opening for access, and states no swing radius.
How the published depth of 16.9 in relates to a real counter: the Emeril is the deepest of the three by 3.5 in against the 6 Qt model, and a standard counter is not generous with that difference.

blocks.html: The first two are left blank on our tables. A dash is an answer: it says the manufacturer page does not state it, and you should get the number from the manual or from the brand before ordering. The third is arithmetic on two published figures, not a new claim.

The 6 Qt is the one to put on a short shelf: 10.63 in tall, against 13.5 in on the 8 Qt and 14.8 in on the oven. Weight is nearly a wash - 13.3 lb against 12.8 lb, with the oven unpublished - so if the machine is going up and down between uses, the height number matters more than the scale.

guides.title: 24 presets or 25? A field guide to spec-sheet drift on appliance pages
guides.meta_description: Two official pages, two preset counts, two model numbers and one wattage that changed between sources. How to read an appliance listing when the manufacturer contradicts itself.
guides.target_query: why do product specifications differ between amazon and manufacturer
guides.hook: The Emeril oven's Amazon title says 24 one-touch preset options. Its own product page says 25 cooking pre-sets in one tile and describes a 10-in-1 oven in the paragraph below. The model number on the store page ends in 02A; the one in the Amazon specification block ends in 02X. This is not a scandal - it is normal, it is everywhere, and once you can see it you cannot shop the same way again.
guides.angle: We found these three drifts by transcribing both pages row by row for our own table. This article is the method, shown on the machine where we found the most of it.

sections.h2: Three drifts on one product

blocks.caption: Every disagreement we published for the 26 Qt oven, with both statements verbatim.
head: Attribute
Manufacturer page

blocks.html: Note the third row: it is not a conflict, it is a gap. Sources disagree and sources are silent, and those are different findings that most write-ups blur into one. On this site they get different labels - CONFLICT and UNVERIFIED.

sections.h2: Why it drifts

blocks.html: A manufacturer's product page is edited by the brand's own commerce team and revised whenever the template changes; an Amazon listing carries a title written for search and a specification block filled in by whoever supplied the data, sometimes years earlier. Neither is wrong on its own terms. Both are documents with a history, and a history is something a buyer can read.

items: Check the count against the feature list, not the headline: 25 pre-sets and a 10-in-1 oven are two different claims about two different things.
Check the model number against the box, not the tile. A suffix difference of one character is usually a variant or a revision, and only one of them will be printed on your machine.
Where a specification is stated by only one of the two sources, note which one said it. The wattage above comes from Amazon's block, not from the brand.

sections.h2: How we handle it here

blocks.html: A conflict is published as a conflict, in the table, with both sources linked. It is never averaged, never quietly dropped, and never resolved by picking the number that reads better. That is also why the site's own open-items page exists: the reader should be able to audit the desk as well as the product.

This is the article a brand will not link to and a reader will remember. Spec-sheet drift is the most useful, least contested thing an affiliate site can write about, because it is a problem the reader already half-senses and no source solves for them.

guides.title: Air fryer vs your oven: what three spec sheets can settle, and what they cannot
guides.meta_description: Air fryer or your oven? The verified numbers for three real machines - capacity, power, temperature - plus the blank column this comparison needs most. Sources on every row.
guides.hook: 'Air fryer vs oven' is really three questions wearing one coat. The three machines on this site are two basket fryers and a 26 Qt countertop oven with French doors, and they answer it three different ways. Here is what their official pages actually settle - and the one appliance in this comparison nobody on this site has read a line about: yours.
guides.angle: Every version of this comparison averages an imaginary oven. We compare only machines whose official pages we have read row by row, and we leave your oven's column blank on purpose: an unpublished number is not a small number, it is an absent one.

sections.h2: The decision, up front

blocks.html: If weeknight dinner is fries, wings, fillets or reheated pizza for one to four people, this comparison points to a basket fryer. If the question is whether to turn on a full-size oven for a family roast, nothing on this page replaces it - the 26 Qt French-door oven comes closest, and closest is still 24.6 litres.

All three machines state the same power draw: 1700 W at 120 V. The difference between them is not watts. It is the shape and volume of the space the watts heat - two independent 3 Qt baskets, one 7.57-litre basket, or a 26 Qt / 24.6-litre cavity that its manufacturer sizes for a whole chicken or a 12-inch pizza.

sections.h2: What the three machines publish, side by side

blocks.html: One number in that table deserves distrust. The Chefman 8 Qt's Amazon title advertises a 450 F Hi-Fry, but the same page's specification block and Chefman's own product page both state 200-400 F for this model. The 450 F maximum is real - it belongs to the 6 Qt dual-window unit. The claim is published as a conflict, not smoothed over.

The Emeril's Amazon product-information block gives 75-500 F, the widest published range of the three, and its manufacturer page lists ten named cooking modes - Air Fry, Bake, Broil, Defrost, Dehydrate, Grill, Proof, Reheat, Roast, Warm.

sections.h2: Your oven, in the column that stays blank

blocks.caption: The comparison as far as the evidence goes. The third column is yours, and no page read for this site publishes a line of it.

blocks.html: The blank column is the point. Your oven's capacity, calibration and insulation are printed on a plate inside its door, not on any page read for this site. Find that plate, measure the cavity, and the comparison becomes real - until then, anyone filling that column with a number is guessing on your behalf.

sections.h2: When the countertop oven is the middle answer

blocks.html: The Emeril is not a basket fryer with a bigger badge. Its published shape is a countertop oven: dual French doors, 360-degree hot-air circulation with a dual-speed fan, ten named cooking modes including Bake, Roast, Proof and Warm, and seven accessories of which the manufacturer names an air fry basket, a rotisserie spit and a bake pan. The accessory count ships as partial: the page says seven and names three.

If the question behind 'air fryer vs oven' is really 'can I skip heating the big oven on a Tuesday', the 26 Qt is the only machine on this page that answers with oven geometry. If the question is 'can I crisp a plate of fries before the big oven finishes preheating', the basket machines answer with a cavity that has almost nothing to preheat. Both answers are about shape, not magic.

sections.h2: What no page here can settle

items: Whether an air fryer meal costs less to run than an oven meal. No official page here publishes watt-hours per cook, so the question stays open on the queue rather than answered here.
Whether food from these machines tastes better. Nobody on this site has cooked in any of them.
Whether 450 F changes what you cook. The temperature is a published row; its effect on dinner is not.
What any of this costs. Prices are withheld on every page of this site by programme rule, and star ratings are not printed because they change faster than a page.

sections.h2: Three questions, then you are done

items: How many people does one meal feed in your house? If the answer is often four or more and the meal is a roast, none of these replaces your oven.
Is the food you would actually cook small and fast - fries, wings, fillets, pizza slices - or large and slow - whole birds, trays, bakes?
What does the counter say? The published footprints are 13.38 x 11.81 x 10.63 in for the 6 Qt, 15.4 x 12.6 x 13.5 in for the 8 Qt, and 16.9 x 15.8 x 14.8 in for the 26 Qt.

blocks.html: Answer those three and the versus question answers itself. The machine that fits the answers is the one worth it - for you, this month, in your kitchen.

guides.title: Are air fryers worth it? What three spec sheets support - and what they never will
guides.meta_description: Are air fryers worth it? No hype and no invented verdicts - the verified specs of three real machines, where the trend outruns its own evidence, and the questions no spec sheet answers.
guides.hook: A verdict on 'worth it' is always really a price, a habit and a kitchen. This site can print none of those. What it can do is strip the trend to its checkable parts: what these three machines state on their official pages, which claims the pages themselves contradict, and who each size is actually built for.
guides.angle: Most 'are they worth it' articles sell a feeling next to a star rating. This one publishes the decision structure instead: every number carries its official page, conflicts stay conflicts, and the value judgement is labelled as a judgement every time it appears.

sections.h2: The honest answer, up front

blocks.html: An air fryer is worth it when the meal you actually cook is small, fast and repeated. It is not worth it when you are hoping it replaces an oven for large or slow cooking. Of the three machines here, two are built for the first meal and one straddles both. That is the whole verdict, and it stays conditional on your kitchen, not on the trend.

The checkable part of the trend is on the pages: 1700 W at 120 V in all three machines, cavities of 6 Qt in two baskets, 7.57 L in one basket, and 26 Qt / 24.6 L behind French doors, and published temperature ranges of 200-450 F, 200-400 F and 75-500 F. Those are the numbers the trend is standing on.

items: '450 F Hi-Fry' is a real published maximum on the 6 Qt dual-window model, and a marketing title borrowed by the 8 Qt, whose own pages stop at 400 F.
The Emeril's model number is published two ways: 4-00675-02A-VN on the manufacturer's store, 4-00675-02X-VN in the Amazon product-information block.

blocks.html: A star rating appears nowhere on this site. Ratings move hourly, they are storefront-specific, and what a static page may claim about them is governed by programme rules. The blank row is the honest row - and it is also why this page can tell you what a machine is, but never whether the crowd loves it.

sections.h2: Who each machine is actually for

blocks.html: The 6 Qt dual-basket is built for cooking two things at once and having them finish together - Sync Finish is the published answer to the nuggets being done before the fries. Two 3 Qt baskets, dual viewing windows with an interior light, nonstick dishwasher-safe baskets.

The 8 Qt TurboFry Touch is the straightforward one: one large basket, four presets, an LED shake reminder, auto shut-off when the timer ends or the basket opens, and a dishwasher-safe basket and rack that the manufacturer marks top-rack.

The 26 Qt French-door oven is the four-to-six-person machine: a cavity sized for a whole chicken or a 12-inch pizza, modes that include Bake, Roast, Proof and Warm, and an accessory set that names a rotisserie spit and a bake pan among its seven pieces.

Match the machine to the meal you cook on a Tuesday, not to the meal you would cook if you cooked more. A 26 Qt oven bought for hypothetical roasts and used for frozen pizza is the most expensive way to reheat pizza.

sections.h2: The questions that decide 'worth it', and why none is answered here

items: What it costs to run. No official page publishes watt-hours per meal, and this site does not estimate.
What the food tastes like. Nobody here has cooked in any of these machines.
What it costs to buy. Prices are withheld on every page of this site by programme rule - the product links carry live prices only where Amazon serves them.
Whether the habit survives month three. That is a question about you, and the buying guide asks it before you spend anything.
Whether the dishwasher note on your machine's care label matches the product page. The pages say dishwasher-safe; the manual is the document that settles it, and it is not on the product pages.

sections.h2: If you want the decision in three minutes

items: Choosing between two baskets and one big one? The duo guide has the trade in numbers.
Measuring the counter first? The fit guide prints the footprints, in inches, with their sources.
Still translating quarts into people? The capacity guide does the arithmetic on all three pages.
Want one machine named rather than three described? That is what the buying guide is for.

blocks.html: 'Worth it' is not a property of an air fryer. It is the gap between the meals you actually cook and the machine you would buy for them. Close that gap with the three questions above and any of these three is worth it. Buy against the trend and none of them is.

prompt_brief.title: The design prompt, as it should read next time
prompt_brief.note: Feed this block to whoever designs the next revision. It is written so a model cannot quietly reintroduce the habits that made the previous version read as generated. Every constraint below is either an editorial standard or a rule the programme already imposes on this site.
blocks: You are designing a niche consumer publication that earns affiliate revenue, not a dashboard and not a landing page for a tool.
A person one decision away from buying an air fryer, arriving from a question, in a hurry, on a phone, sceptical of praise.
Move the reader from a question to a decision in one scroll, then hand them to the listing. Everything else on the page exists to make that decision trustworthy.
Short declarative sentences. Numbers where adjectives would go. A stated opinion, in a labelled box, separated from the measurements. No hedging in circles: state a limit once, plainly, then move on.

Scene-setting openers, category eulogies, whether you are a X or a Y, three-card hero rows, and any sentence that would survive being pasted into an article about a kettle. The banned list is enforced by the build, and the list grows from rejects, not from taste.

Every factual sentence carries a citation that resolves to a manufacturer page or an Amazon listing. A blank row shows the reason for the blank. A disagreement between two sources is shown as a disagreement, with both, and states which number we use.

Paper white, ink black, one rust accent, hairline rules, a serif for article titles, tabular numerals, no photography, no shadows, no gradients, no icons in circles, no carousels, no modals, no newsletter popup.

The disclosure sentence on every page, a clear paid-link marker beside every product link, rel=sponsored on every outbound marketplace link, no price and no star rating anywhere, and no Amazon mark in our own naming. These are enforced by the deploy gate, not by memory.

A hub per cluster; guides that answer one search phrasing each; a per-model write-up; one comparison table that is the same data in a different shape. Every guide links to two others and to the buying guide. Sitemap and canonical tags on, Article and BreadcrumbList markup only.
One static sub-tag per article once an Associates ID exists, so the outcome is visible per page. No user-derived tagging.
A reader who has never heard of the site can name the model that fits their kitchen and say why. If the page could be about any brand, it is not finished.

before_after.problem: The generated opener - a category eulogy that could preface any product on the internet.
before_after.before: In today's fast-paced world, air fryers have revolutionized the way we cook. From crispy fries to juicy chicken, these versatile appliances deliver healthy, delicious meals with ease. In this article, we'll delve into the top features that make this air fryer a must-have for any kitchen.
before_after.after: Six quarts is not a family size, and the manufacturer page does not claim it is. It is two 3-quart baskets with a function that ends them at the same moment - which is an answer to a different question than how much food you cook.
before_after.fix: V-01 (open on the decision), V-04 (no hype verbs), V-02 (the first sentence is checkable).

before_after.problem: An unfalsifiable superlative doing the work a measurement should do.
before_after.before: This cutting-edge appliance boasts an impressive temperature range and seamless controls for top-notch results.
before_after.after: 200 to 450 F, with the top of the range reached in Hi-Fry. The control type is a digital touchscreen; the listing says so, the manufacturer's feature list gives the range.
before_after.fix: V-04 (no superlatives), V-07 (concrete nouns), V-02 (source beside the number).

before_after.problem: A limitation written as a legal disclaimer, three sentences deep, so the reader skips it.
before_after.before: Please note that the information provided herein is subject to change and may not reflect current manufacturer specifications. We encourage all readers to verify details directly with the manufacturer prior to making a purchase decision.
before_after.after: Specifications change. This page was read on 15 November 2026, and the links go to the pages we read.
before_after.fix: V-05 (name the gap, once), V-06 (one idea per sentence).

before_after.problem: Praise substituted for a recommendation, so nobody can act on it.
before_after.before: Overall, this air fryer is an excellent choice for anyone looking to elevate their culinary experience. We highly recommend it!
before_after.after: Buy it if two dishes need to finish together. Skip it if you cook one large batch for four to six people - the 8 Qt single chamber is the larger volume, and the 26 Qt oven is the one that roasts.
before_after.fix: V-08 (say who it is not for), V-03 (the opinion is labelled, and it is an opinion).

next_articles_note: Six candidates, each naming the gap that blocks it, are published on the board under DS-14.

P1.verdict: Two baskets, not one big one. The published argument for this machine is a function rather than a volume: Sync Finish ends both 3 Qt baskets at the same moment, and the top of its range is 450 F in Hi-Fry. If your problem is two dishes on one counter, that is the specification to shop for. If your problem is one large batch, the 8 Qt model has the bigger chamber.
buy_if: You cook two different things at once and want them on the table together.
You want to see the food without pulling a drawer: the manufacturer prints dual viewing windows and an interior light.
Your shelf clearance is tight. At 10.63 in tall it is the shortest of the three.
skip_if: You need a single chamber that takes a whole tray. Each basket here is 3 Qt.
You have no width to spare: 13.38 in across, 13.3 lb to lift onto the shelf afterwards.
P1.gap: Neither official page states an inner-basket material or a minimum clearance, so those rows are blank rather than guessed.

P2.verdict: A small convection oven that also air fries, and the door is the reason to buy it. French doors open onto a 26 Qt chamber 16.9 in deep with a published 75-500 F range: low enough to dehydrate, high enough to roast. A basket fryer cannot take a sheet pan. This can, and that is the counter space worth paying for.
buy_if: You cook for four to six people, which is what the manufacturer's own capacity tile states.
You want one appliance to stand in for a second oven: ten published modes, proof through broil.
You have 16.9 in of counter depth and 14.8 in of height to give.
You want rotisserie without a second appliance: the manufacturer names a rotisserie spit among the seven accessories it counts in the box.
skip_if: Your real need is a fast reheat. A basket heats far less empty air.
You cannot give up the counter permanently: at 14.8 in tall, this is a machine you move with intent.
P2.gap: Two counts stay unresolved on the brand's own page - the listing title says 24 presets, the specification tile says 25, and the paragraph under it calls it 10-in-1. The store page and Amazon's block also carry different model suffixes. Both versions are printed and marked CONFLICT.

P3.verdict: The largest single chamber of the three at 8 Qt, on the same 1700 W as its smaller sibling, with a four-preset panel that asks nothing of you. Its published range stops at 400 F, which is the one number worth arguing about, because the Amazon title for the same model advertises 450 F.
buy_if: You cook one large batch for four to six people, which the page states as the design target.
You want the shortest decision available: four presets, an LED shake reminder, and a documented auto shut-off.
The basket is going in the dishwasher - the page says basket and rack, top rack.
skip_if: You need a 450 F finishing stage. The manufacturer specification for this model states 200-400 F.
You need to watch the food. No window is claimed on this page.
P3.gap: One manufacturer URL sells both the 5 Qt and the 8 Qt model. Every row in this table is the 8 Qt variant, checked against the size selector on the page.

voice_pass_merge.what: The 2026-11-15 voice pass (session 8c4236ad, PR #75) added reader-facing fields ending in `_editorial` to `marketing/data/facts.json`. They are carried, not dropped: `hook_editorial` is the one-line summary on the product-articles index; `look_elsewhere` renders as each product page's 'Elsewhere on this site' list; `planned_topics` renders on the guides index with a crosswalk to what covers each entry; and eight of the nine `suits_editorial` lines were already carried, with figures attached, by `buy_if` below - the ninth, the rotisserie spit, is now there too. Article ledes stay on `verdict`, because the same sentence cannot be written twice; where the two files frame a product differently, the spec table in `facts.json` is the tie-breaker, which is also that pass's own rule.

trending.title: Trending topics, and what would keep them honest
trending.lede: Article shapes this set could grow into, carried over from the 2026-11-15 marketing pass (session bf8f07a7, PR #65) and kept here in the generator so the page gets the same masthead, disclosure and sourcing rules as everything else. Each is a proposal. None is commissioned, and none of them changes a single verified value.
trending.how_label: Editorial hypothesis — how a page like this earns a reader, not a measured result
how: Answer one specific question in the title and keep the promise in the first screen. A page about what 6 Qt actually holds beats a page called 'Top Air Fryers' for a reader who already knows what they are asking.
Lead with numbers the manufacturer printed. Specificity is the only thing a reader can check here, so it is also the only thing worth building a headline on.
Compare rather than describe. Someone choosing between two baskets and one big basket is closer to a decision than someone browsing a list, and a decision is the moment a link gets clicked.

Put the boring parts in the same page: what the cavity measures, whether it fits the counter, what happens when two official pages disagree. That is what an article can do that a listing page will not.
Keep internal links deliberate — guide to article, article to guide — so a reader who finishes one page has an obvious next question to ask.
Disclose plainly and mark paid links, which Google's own guidance asks for on sponsored links and the Associates agreement requires regardless.
trending.queue_intro: Each row is a proposal, not a commission, and the queue is decided on the improvement board (DS-14 and the question register) — a list nobody prioritises is just a list.

queue.title: Best dual-basket air fryer for a family of four

queue.title: Does an air fryer cost less to run than an oven?
queue.angle: Every one of these three draws 1700 W on its own page, so the honest version of this piece is about how long a run takes and what preheating costs, not about a machine that is cheaper to run. Electricity price is regional and is not ours to state.

queue.title: Choosing capacity: the measurement behind the number
queue.angle: Quarts are a volume, not a serving count, and the three products state household size differently — the useful article is the one that shows the arithmetic.

trending.gate_intro: Before any of these becomes a page, the same five checks apply that the 2026-11-15 pass wrote, kept because they are the right gates:
gate: Propose it on the improvement board with its options and its cost, so the owner chooses a path before anything is built.
Do not let the article imply that the observed destination is the product the brief named. Identity is unconfirmed (F-03), and every page carries that sentence.
Build every specification row from a manufacturer or Amazon page. Leave blanks blank; never infer a value to fill a column.
Mark each marketplace link paid, and keep the disclosure inside the same container as the link.
Date-stamp the read and re-read the page before republication, so a silent change on the source cannot pass as our mistake.

No verified value was added, removed or changed.
